Chapter 8: Facing the Nation’s Fault Lines—Race, War, and the Limits of Power.
Running for president in 1968 meant coming face-to-face with America’s deepest wounds. Just imagine it. The Vietnam War wasn’t just a headline—it was raging on, tearing families apart, and splitting the nation in two. Cities weren’t just restless; they were erupting in protest and sometimes even violence. And underneath it all, racial tensions simmered, sometimes boiling over into heartbreak and tragedy.
Right in the middle of this storm was Bobby Kennedy. He found himself trying to bridge divides that, to many, seemed impossible to cross.
Picture him visiting college campuses, where students demanded an end to the war. He listened to veterans, men and women haunted by memories they could never shake. He met with mothers who had lost their sons, and with activists who’d lost hope. The war wasn’t some abstract policy debate—it was, at its core, a human catastrophe. And Bobby’s opposition to it? It only grew sharper. He called for a negotiated peace. He pleaded for an end to the killing. He urged a new way of thinking—one rooted in understanding, not just in force.
But war wasn’t the only fault line. Race cut just as deep. After Dr. King’s assassination, it felt like the country was on the brink of tearing itself apart. Bobby didn’t just speak out for justice—he called for reconciliation. He met with Black leaders, community organizers, young people who were angry at a system that kept failing them. He never claimed to have all the answers. Instead, he offered something just as important—solidarity. He acknowledged the pain, the anger, the long and painful history of injustice. And he urged Americans to see one another not as enemies, but as neighbors.
There were moments when the limits of power became painfully clear. Bobby couldn’t bring back the dead, or erase centuries of inequality. He couldn’t end the war with a single speech, or heal every wound overnight. But you know what he could do? He could bear witness. He could listen. And where he could, he acted. He pushed for policies to fight poverty, to expand opportunity, to protect civil rights. He challenged the comfortable, the powerful, the complacent.
The campaign trail was a crucible. Bobby was tested—by hecklers, by threats, by the relentless grind of public life. He was sometimes impatient, sometimes exhausted, sometimes just overwhelmed by how much needed fixing. But he didn’t stop. He kept going, driven by this deep sense that the country needed healing—and that he, somehow, had a part to play.
